readings.title: Frederick Douglass
readings.challenge: Follow images of battle and mourning through a long, formal elegy.
readings.focus: An elegy that grieves a leader also turns grief into a promise to continue his work.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), the son of parents who had been enslaved, wrote this elegy in 1895, the year Frederick Douglass died. Douglass had escaped slavery and became the most famous abolitionist speaker and writer in America. The lists are the fenced ground of a tournament; Ethiopia stands for Africa and its descendants, as it often did then; a clarion is a trumpet; imprecations are curses.
readings.contentNote: Slavery, the lash and oppression appear in figurative language.

excerpt.locator: “Frederick Douglass,” complete poem; opens “A hush is over all the teeming lists, And there is pause, a breath-space in the strife; A…”; closes “…And, rising from beneath the chast'ning rod, She stretches out her bleeding hands to God!”.

questions.prompt: Who mourns Douglass in the first two stanzas, and how is that mourner pictured?
facilitatorNotes: Ethiopia, as a mother weeping for her son “with bosom torn.” The poem makes Douglass the child of a whole people, not only of a family.
evidence: And Ethiopia, with bosom torn,
She weeps for him a mother's burning tears--

questions.prompt: Find the weapons and battle words. What kind of fighter was Douglass, according to the poem?
facilitatorNotes: His voice is a trumpet, his words are arrows sent into Oppression’s den, he answers thunder with thunder and dies “with his armor on.” His weapons are speech and truth.
evidence: For her his voice, a fearless clarion, rung
And answered thunder with his thunder back.

questions.prompt: “He was no soft-tongued apologist.” What does the line praise, and what does it hint about other speakers?
facilitatorNotes: He named wrongs plainly instead of excusing or softening them. The line implies that others did soften their words to please listeners, which makes his plainness a kind of courage.
evidence: And he was no soft-tongued apologist;
He spoke straightforward, fearlessly uncowed;

questions.prompt: How do the last two stanzas turn from grief toward the future?
facilitatorNotes: The mourners have “touched his hand” and promise to “triumph yet” under his banner. The final picture of bleeding hands stretched to God joins suffering and hope; readers may find the ending confident or still sorrowful.
evidence: O'er all that holds us we shall triumph yet,
She stretches out her bleeding hands to God!

readings.title: The Old Apple-Tree
readings.challenge: Follow one memory through the stages of a life, and notice how the speaker answers a listener’s doubt.
readings.focus: An ugly old tree is the dearest in the orchard because a whole life has been lived around it.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote in standard English and in several dialects; this poem uses the country speech of the Midwest, where he grew up. An old man remembers by the fire. Verdant means green; a sanctum is a private room; sugared nonsense is sweet, silly talk.

excerpt.locator: “The Old Apple-Tree,” complete poem; opens “There's a memory keeps a-runnin' Through my weary head to-night, An' I see a picture…”; closes “…my last request shall be,-- That they 'll bury me an' Hallie 'Neath the old apple tree.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker admit about how the tree looks to a stranger?
facilitatorNotes: Its boughs are gnarled and crooked, its leaves thin, its harvest smaller: “You perhaps would call it ugly.” He grants the point, then insists it is still the dearest, so its value comes from memory, not looks.
evidence: You perhaps would call it ugly,
Unadorned by memory's glow;

questions.prompt: Trace the stages of the speaker’s life that happened in or under the tree.
facilitatorNotes: Reading in its shelter, swinging on its boughs as a boy, courting Hallie on the seat beneath it, growing old with her, and finally wishing to be buried there. The tree holds childhood, love, marriage and death.
evidence: It's the place where me an' Hallie--
That they 'll bury me an' Hallie

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza mix happiness and sorrow? Is the ending sad?
facilitatorNotes: He admits life “ain't all been summer” yet says their load was never too heavy to carry; the burial wish puts death beside the place of their courtship. Some readers find it peaceful, others melancholy.
evidence: Life for us ain't all been summer,
That we longed to lay it down.

readings.title: An Ante-Bellum Sermon
readings.challenge: Hear two messages in one sermon and notice how the preacher protects himself.
readings.focus: A Bible story becomes a hidden hope for freedom, preached where those who would punish it may be listening.
readings.context: Ante-bellum means before the Civil War. In this dialect poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar, an enslaved preacher speaks to his congregation about Moses leading the Hebrews out of slavery in Egypt, a story enslaved people often told about their own hopes. The vials of power are the plagues; brigity means bold or uppity; reco'nised ez citiz' means recognised as citizens.
readings.contentNote: Set among enslaved people; mentions chains, shackles and masters. Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “An Ante-Bellum Sermon,” complete poem; opens “We is gathahed hyeah, my brothahs, In dis howlin' wildaness, Fu' to speak some words of…”; closes “…mighty reck'nin' day, When we 'se reco'nised ez citiz'-- Huh uh! Chillun, let us pray!”.

questions.prompt: What Bible story does the preacher tell, and what does it say about God and slavery?
facilitatorNotes: God sends Moses to tell Pharaoh to free the Hebrew children, punishes Pharaoh when he refuses, and frees them. In the story God sides with the enslaved.
evidence: Fu' to let dem chillun go.
But de Lawd will sen' some Moses

questions.prompt: Why does the preacher keep stopping to say he is talking only about ancient times? Do you believe him?
facilitatorNotes: He fears someone will tell the masters he is “preachin' discontent.” The denials are a shield, and each one also points straight at the real meaning, so most readers hear irony.
evidence: I ain't talkin' 'bout to-day.
Dat I's preachin' discontent.

questions.prompt: How does the preacher use the Bible as evidence against slavery?
facilitatorNotes: God made “Evah mothah's son” free, and Scripture says a servant is worthy of his hire, so anyone who defends slavery must call the Scripture a liar. He argues from the masters’ own sacred book.
evidence: Evah mothah's son was free.
But dey calls de Scriptuah liar,

questions.prompt: What is the preacher about to say in the last lines, and why does he stop?
facilitatorNotes: He begins to say they will be recognised as citizens, then breaks off into prayer. He has said openly what he has been hinting, and he retreats at once; the break is both comic and tense.
evidence: When we 'se reco'nised ez citiz'--
Huh uh! Chillun, let us pray!

readings.title: Ode to Ethiopia
readings.challenge: Follow the ode from past to present to future, and weigh what it chooses to praise.
readings.focus: A young poet tells his people to be proud: of surviving slavery, of their work and voices now, and of the story still to come.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), the son of parents who had been enslaved, printed this ode in his first book of poems, when he was about twenty. An ode is a formal poem of praise addressed to its subject. As in many writings of his time, Ethiopia stands for Africa and all people of African descent, so “Ethiope’s children” are Black Americans. Swarthy means dark-skinned and fairer means lighter-skinned; senate halls are lawmaking assemblies, where Black men served after the Civil War; blazoned means proudly displayed; the rack was an instrument of torture; chrism is holy oil used in blessing; a lyre is a harp.
readings.contentNote: Slavery’s cruelty appears in figurative language (“dear blood all gory,” “the rack”). The poem uses the period words “swarthy” and “fairer” for skin colour.

excerpt.locator: “Ode to Ethiopia,” complete poem; opens “O Mother Race! to thee I bring This pledge of faith unwavering, This tribute to thy…”; closes “…who from thy root shall spring, And proudly tune their lyres to sing Of Ethiopia's glory.”.

questions.prompt: The ode moves through time. Which stanzas look back, which describe the present, and which look ahead?
facilitatorNotes: The first two look back at slavery and the slow growth of freedom; the third and fourth show the present; the fifth to seventh explain why pride is earned; the last turns to the future with “Go on and up!” and the poets still to be born. The shape tells a story of rising.
evidence: When Slavery crushed thee with its heel,
Go on and up! Our souls and eyes

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza tell history through the growth of a plant? Why might Dunbar choose a plant rather than, say, a battle?
facilitatorNotes: Even in the sad days a seed of better times was growing; freedom sprang up, put out young leaves and is now in blossom. Growth is slow, living and hard to stop, and the young leaves suggest that freedom is still new. A battle would stress violence; the plant stresses patience and life.
evidence: But through the land the fruitful seed Of better times was growing.
The plant of freedom upward sprung,

questions.prompt: In the third and fourth stanzas, what are Black Americans shown doing? Why might Dunbar list these things in the 1890s?
facilitatorNotes: Clearing forests, hammering at forges, working the fields, speaking in senate halls, singing hymns: labour, citizenship and faith. Many white Americans then claimed that freed people could not make their own way; the list answers them, and places Black citizens “Beside” their neighbours as equals.
evidence: Their hammers ring, their forges smoke,--
Their voices sound through senate halls

questions.prompt: Dunbar says no other race, when free, was “So noble in forgiving.” What might a reader admire in this claim, and what might trouble them?
facilitatorNotes: Admire: the dignity and moral strength it honours, linked to the cross and holy oil of the sixth stanza. Trouble: praising forgiveness can seem to ask the wronged to carry the burden, and “Forgot the past” sits oddly beside an opening that insists on remembering. Accept answers on either side that use the lines.
evidence: No other race, when free again, Forgot the past and proved them men So noble in forgiving.

readings.title: The Master-Player
readings.challenge: Read a short allegory, in which feelings act like people, and decide what its objects stand for.
readings.focus: Joy, Hate and Fear cannot draw music from a worn-out harp; only Love can.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), the son of parents who had been enslaved in Kentucky, grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and became one of the best-known American poets of his time. In this poem, as in an allegory, feelings appear as musicians. Frayed means worn into loose threads; essayed means tried; responsiveness is the quality of answering; undismayed means not discouraged; to smite is to strike.

excerpt.locator: “The Master-Player,” complete poem; opens “An old, worn harp that had been played Till all its strings were loose and frayed, Joy,…”; closes “…Smote on its strings, still strange to song, And brought forth music sweet and strong.”.

questions.prompt: Who tries to play the old harp first, and what happens?
facilitatorNotes: Joy, Hate and Fear each try, and none gets a “sweet” sound from it. It is surprising that even Joy fails; ask readers why that might be.
evidence: Joy, Hate, and Fear, each one essayed,
No sweet responsiveness of sound.

questions.prompt: What might the old, worn harp stand for?
facilitatorNotes: Most readers take it as a person, or a heart, worn out by life, so that feelings no longer “play” on it. Some may say a country, a family or a friendship. Any reading should explain the loose, frayed strings.
evidence: An old, worn harp that had been played
Till all its strings were loose and frayed,

questions.prompt: Why does Love succeed where the others fail? Which words show how Love plays?
facilitatorNotes: Love comes passionately (“eyes aflame”), is not put off by the harp’s state, and strikes boldly. The music is “sweet and strong,” as if the worn harp had been made new. Readers may argue about whether love alone can do this.
evidence: The Harp he took all undismayed,
And brought forth music sweet and strong.

readings.title: The Mystery
readings.challenge: Follow unrhymed lines of blank verse whose sentences run across the line-ends, and hear how the poem’s questions go unanswered.
readings.focus: A speaker who cannot see before his birth or after his death searches for a guiding voice and does not find one.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, wrote in many forms. This poem is in blank verse: unrhymed lines of about ten syllables. Fain means gladly; a chart is a map and steel here means a compass needle; to feign is to pretend; to list is to listen; supernal means heavenly; a novice is a beginner.
readings.contentNote: The speaker says he hears no voice of God and cannot know what follows death; other people’s faith is described as possibly pretended.

excerpt.locator: “The Mystery,” complete poem; opens “I was not; now I am--a few days hence I shall not be; I fain would look before And after,…”; closes “…their eyes On me, as I one day shall do on them, And tell me not the secret that I ask.”.

questions.prompt: The first sentence describes a whole life in a few words. What are its three parts?
facilitatorNotes: “I was not” (before birth), “now I am” (life), “I shall not be” (death). The speaker wants to see before and after, and cannot. The short phrases make life seem very brief.
evidence: I was not; now I am--a few days hence
I shall not be; I fain would look before

questions.prompt: What picture does the speaker use for his life? What is missing from it?
facilitatorNotes: A wide, sunless plain with no map or compass, where he can only grope “by chance.” Light, direction and guidance are missing. Ask how this differs from pictures of life as a road or a journey home.
evidence: I stand upon a wide and sunless plain,
Nor chart nor steel to guide my steps aright.

questions.prompt: Some people, he says, “feign to hear a voice and feel a hand.” How is he different from them? Is “feign” fair?
facilitatorNotes: He hears and feels nothing, though he keeps listening and reaching. “Feign” (pretend) may sound harsh to believers; it may also show envy or honest doubt. Notice that he does not stop searching.
evidence: Some feign to hear a voice and feel a hand
But I--I hear no voice and touch no hand,

questions.prompt: The skies “daily shut their eyes / On me, as I one day shall do on them.” What does this comparison suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Night falling is like the sky closing its eyes, and the speaker’s death will be his closing his eyes on the sky. The sky keeps its secret. Some readers find the ending bleak; others find calm in its honesty.
evidence: But they roll on, and daily shut their eyes
And tell me not the secret that I ask.

readings.title: Not They Who Soar
readings.challenge: Follow a contrast between two ways of travelling and decide which one the poem honours.
readings.focus: The poem redefines heroism as hard, unhelped labour on the ground.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar uses an old French form, the rondeau, in which the opening words return as a short refrain. To plod is to walk slowly and heavily; the sod and the clod are the earth; a share is a plough blade.

excerpt.locator: “Not They Who Soar,” complete poem; opens “Not they who soar, but they who plod Their rugged way, unhelped, to God Are heroes; they…”; closes “…flight is ever free and rare; But heroes they the soil who 've trod, Not they who soar!”.

questions.prompt: Who are the heroes in this poem, and who are not?
facilitatorNotes: Those who plod “unhelped” along a rugged way, not those who soar above it. Flight is easy and free; heroism lies in the difficulty.
evidence: Not they who soar, but they who plod
Their rugged way, unhelped, to God

questions.prompt: Which details show the plodders’ hardship, and what might they suggest?
facilitatorNotes: Backs that have “felt the rod,” bare feet, thorns, hidden boulders, the plough. The rod may suggest whipping, and from Dunbar it may recall slavery; readers can discuss how far the poem invites that reading.
evidence: 'Tis they whose backs have felt the rod,
Whose feet have pressed the path unshod,

questions.prompt: Why do the soarers lose something by missing the toil? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: Those who fly never struggle, so they never earn the right to “smile upon defeated care.” The poem implies hardship gives worth or understanding; some readers will question whether suffering always ennobles.
evidence: Miss all the toil that hugs the sod.
May smile upon defeated care,

readings.title: Whittier
readings.challenge: Read a poem about a death that refuses to mourn in the usual way, and find its reason.
readings.focus: Dunbar honours a poet whose life matched his words, and argues that great poets never die.
readings.context: John Greenleaf Whittier (1807–1892) was an American Quaker poet who worked and wrote against slavery for decades; his poems were read in schools across the country. Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, wrote this poem after Whittier’s death. Maudlin means tearfully over-sentimental; drift here means a flow of words; sublime means grand and awe-inspiring; malignant means harmful; “mortal ken” is human sight.

excerpt.locator: “Whittier,” complete poem; opens “Not o'er thy dust let there be spent The gush of maudlin sentiment; Such drift as that is…”; closes “…for evermore-- Though far thy form from mortal ken-- Deep in the hearts and minds of men.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of mourning does the speaker reject, and why is it wrong for Whittier?
facilitatorNotes: A “gush of maudlin sentiment,” showy tears. Whittier’s life, deeds and songs were simple and honest, so gushing grief would be false to him.
evidence: The gush of maudlin sentiment;
Whose life and deeds and songs agree,

questions.prompt: “O singer sweet, thou art not dead!” In what sense is Whittier still alive?
facilitatorNotes: His songs still “thrill” readers, and he lives “in the hearts and minds of men.” The poem says the earth values great poets too much to lose them. Readers can test the claim: whose words still live for them?
evidence: With living fire thy songs shall thrill,
Deep in the hearts and minds of men.

questions.prompt: Why might it matter that a poet’s “life and deeds and songs agree”? What would it mean if they did not?
facilitatorNotes: Whittier’s poems against slavery were matched by his work against it; his words could be trusted. A poet whose life contradicted his poems would seem a hypocrite. Students may think of other people whose words and actions match, or do not.
evidence: Whose life and deeds and songs agree,
Sublime in their simplicity.

readings.title: Keep A-Pluggin’ Away
readings.challenge: Watch how a refrain works, and decide whether the poem’s advice is as simple as it sounds.
readings.focus: A cheerful motto repeated twelve times, with a joke and a hard truth tucked inside it.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar knew about plugging away: after high school he could find no better work than running an elevator in Dayton, Ohio, and he wrote poems between calls and paid to print his first book himself. To plug away is to keep working steadily at something hard. A motto is a short saying to live by; homely means plain and ordinary; to bide one’s time is to wait patiently; to delve is to dig; perseverance is keeping on despite difficulty.

excerpt.locator: “Keep A-Pluggin’ Away,” complete poem; opens “I 've a humble little motto That is homely, though it 's true,-- Keep a-pluggin' away.…”; closes “…king; Time its sure reward will bring; Work and wait unwearying,-- Keep a-pluggin' away.”.

questions.prompt: Count how often the refrain comes. How does the repetition match the advice?
facilitatorNotes: Twelve times, three in every stanza. The poem plugs away itself, steady and stubborn, and the short refrain line after the longer ones lands like a blow of a hammer.
evidence: I 've a humble little motto That is homely, though it 's true,--

questions.prompt: List the troubles the poem expects. Which come from nature, and which from people?
facilitatorNotes: Rising storms, opposing waters, high hills, hard paths, torrents of rain and frowning skies, all pictures of difficulty; and from people, “sneers to swallow.” The poem does not pretend success is easy or quick.
evidence: If the hills are high before And the paths are hard to climb,
There 'll be lots of sneers to swallow,

questions.prompt: “Delve away beneath the surface, / There is treasure farther down.” What might the treasure be for a toiler, a poet or a priest?
facilitatorNotes: For a worker, skill or reward; for a poet, the true poem under the first rough attempts; for a priest, deeper faith. Digging is slow work no one sees, and the treasure stays hidden until you reach it.
evidence: Be thou toiler, poet, priest,
Delve away beneath the surface, There is treasure farther down,--

questions.prompt: Read “If you 've got your eye on heaven, / Some bright day you 'll wake up there.” Is this a promise, a joke, or both?
facilitatorNotes: A promise of reward, and also a sly joke: to wake up in heaven you must first die, so the reward may come very late indeed. Some readers hear only faith; others hear a wry smile at how long “Time” can take to pay.
evidence: If you 've got your eye on heaven, Some bright day you 'll wake up there,--
Time its sure reward will bring;

readings.title: The Colored Soldiers
readings.challenge: Follow an argument addressed to “you” through a poem of praise.
readings.focus: A war song becomes a demand that the nation remember what it owes.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar honours the nearly 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors who fought for the Union in the Civil War. Fort Wagner, Olustee and Fort Pillow were battles of 1863–64; at Fort Pillow, Confederate troops killed many Black soldiers after they had surrendered. “Sons of Ham” is an old biblical name for African peoples, once used to defend slavery, which Dunbar turns into praise. It is read on Veterans Day, which honours everyone who has served in the armed forces.
readings.contentNote: War, wounds and death; refers to the massacre at Fort Pillow; uses historical racial terms.

excerpt.locator: “The Colored Soldiers,” complete poem; opens “If the muse were mine to tempt it And my feeble voice were strong, If my tongue were…”; closes “…glory To those noble sons of Ham-- The gallant colored soldiers Who fought for Uncle Sam!”.

questions.prompt: Who is “you” in the second and third stanzas, and how did “you” first treat the colored soldiers?
facilitatorNotes: The white North and its army, who scorned Black volunteers and called the war “the white man's,” then called on them when the flag was “drooping low.” The poem speaks to those who rejected and then needed them.
evidence: These battles are the white man's,
Then you called the colored soldiers,

questions.prompt: Why does the poem pause on Fort Pillow? How is that stanza different from the others?
facilitatorNotes: It turns from praise to prayer: mercy on the deeds done there and on victims sent “without a prayer.” It names an atrocity without describing it, and the restraint gives it force.
evidence: And at Pillow! God have mercy
Sent to Thee without a prayer.

questions.prompt: “Are they more or less to-day?” What is the poem asking, and why ask it about thirty years after the war?
facilitatorNotes: Whether the nation still treats Black veterans and citizens as comrades and equals. The question challenges readers who praise soldiers’ courage but forget their rights; readers can say what answer the following stanzas imply.
evidence: They were comrades then and brothers,
Are they more or less to-day?

questions.prompt: The poem opens by doubting its own voice. Does that modest beginning fit what follows?
facilitatorNotes: Wishing for the muse and a stronger voice is a traditional modest opening, and the poem then sings the stirring song anyway. Some readers see only a convention, others a real worry about being heard.
evidence: And my feeble voice were strong,

readings.title: October
readings.challenge: Follow one long comparison through three stanzas and notice how it changes at the end.
readings.focus: October is a rich, carefree young woman who spends all her wealth on bright clothes and does not care when Frost arrives.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and wrote many poems about the seasons of the Midwest. A treasurer looks after money; bounty is generous gifts and tribute is payment owed to a ruler; coffers are money chests; lavishness is generous spending; gaudy means showy; roguish means mischievous; demeanor is manner; auburn is reddish-brown, and locks are hair.

excerpt.locator: “October,” complete poem; opens “October is the treasurer of the year, And all the months pay bounty to her store; The…”; closes “…joyously, Nor cares when Frost stalks o'er her way And turns her auburn locks to gray.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza turn October into a person? Where does her wealth come from, and how does she spend it?
facilitatorNotes: She is “the treasurer of the year”: the harvest from fields and orchards fills her coffers. She spends it all on “gaudy dress” of scarlet, purple and gold, which is the autumn leaves.
evidence: October is the treasurer of the year,
Spends all her wealth in gaudy dress,

questions.prompt: What are the “pearls of early dew,” and who steals them?
facilitatorNotes: Drops of dew caught on her trailing garments, the plants of the woodland; the “roguish Sun” steals them by drying them up in the morning. The poem makes an ordinary morning into a small comedy.
evidence: And gather pearls of early dew
Creeps up and steals them every one.

questions.prompt: What happens to October at the end, and why does she not care? Do you admire her?
facilitatorNotes: Frost turns her “auburn locks to gray”: the leaves wither and winter comes. She has lived “joyously” and has no regrets. Some readers admire her freedom; others see a warning about spending everything at once.
evidence: Whole-hearted, happy, careless, free,
And turns her auburn locks to gray.

readings.title: Ships That Pass in the Night
readings.challenge: Read an extended metaphor and decide what the ship might stand for.
readings.focus: A desperate cry to a passing ship expresses longing for something just out of reach.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar takes his title from a phrase of Longfellow’s for people who meet once and pass on. Pregnant night is night full of what is about to happen; glassing here means mirroring; a bark is a ship.

excerpt.locator: “Ships That Pass in the Night,” complete poem; opens “Out in the sky the great dark clouds are massing; I look far out into the pregnant night,…”; closes “…may sight and check that speeding bark Which out of sight and sound is passing, passing?”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker actually see and hear of the ship?
facilitatorNotes: Only a booming gun and a random gleam of light; the ship itself is never seen. The speaker follows it through faint signs.
evidence: Where I can hear a solemn booming gun

questions.prompt: What happens when the speaker calls out? Why is that image so painful?
facilitatorNotes: The voice “falls dead a foot from mine own lips,” and only its ghost reaches the ship. The speaker cannot even be heard; the effort fails almost at once.
evidence: My voice falls dead a foot from mine own lips,
And but its ghost doth reach that vessel

questions.prompt: What could the “ship of ships” stand for? Support one reading and acknowledge another.
facilitatorNotes: A lost love, a chance, success, faith or hope; the poem never says. The repeated “passing, passing” at the end of each stanza stresses that it is going and will not return.
evidence: For I would hail and check that ship of ships.
Which out of sight and sound is passing, passing?

readings.title: When Malindy Sings
readings.challenge: Hear a speaker’s argument about music and judge how fair it is.
readings.focus: Natural, heartfelt singing is set above trained, book-learned music.
readings.context: In this dialect poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar, the speaker tells Miss Lucy, who is practising from a music book, that no training can match Malindy’s singing. Melojous means melodious; heish means hush; “Come to Jesus” and “Rock of Ages” are hymns, and “Swing Low, Sweet Chariot” is a spiritual.
readings.contentNote: Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “When Malindy Sings,” complete poem; opens “G'way an' quit dat noise, Miss Lucy-- Put dat music book away; What's de use to keep on…”; closes “…de bresh of angels' wings, Sof an' sweet, "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot," Ez Malindy sings.”.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker’s complaint about Miss Lucy’s singing?
facilitatorNotes: She reads “lines an' dots” but lacks the natural voice and the turns and twistings of real singing; practising until she is gray will not help. The speaker sets feeling and gift above notation.
evidence: Put dat music book away;
Lookin' at de lines an' dots,

questions.prompt: How does the poem show the power of Malindy’s voice without our hearing it?
facilitatorNotes: By its effects: birds hush and hide, fiddlers and banjo players stop, sinners tremble toward the hymn, listeners cry. Everyone else’s response proves her art.
evidence: Heish dey moufs an' hides dey faces
An' you fin' yo' teahs a-drappin'

questions.prompt: Who is the expert in this poem? Does the speaker convince you that training cannot compete?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker claims to know real singing better than the girl with the music book, quietly reversing who usually teaches whom. Readers may still argue that training and natural gift need not be rivals.
evidence: When hit comes to raal right singin',
'T ain't no easy thing to do.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza the speaker hushes the dog and the child. What does that show about how the poem ends?
facilitatorNotes: Malindy is singing right now, and the speaker wants silence to listen. The poem ends in the present moment, as if we might hear her too, with the spiritual drifting from valley to hill.
evidence: Towsah, stop dat ba'kin', hyeah me!
Ez Malindy sings.

readings.title: Sympathy
readings.challenge: Follow the three things the speaker knows and how the refrain changes.
readings.focus: A caged bird’s song is revealed as a prayer from pain, not a sign of joy.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar, the son of parents who had been enslaved, published this poem in 1899. Opes means opens; a chalice is a cup, here a flower’s; fain means gladly; a carol is a joyful song.
readings.contentNote: A caged bird bloodies its wings against the bars; the suffering is figurative.

excerpt.locator: “Sympathy,” complete poem; opens “I know what the caged bird feels, alas! When the sun is bright on the upland slopes; When…”; closes “…deep core, But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings-- I know why the caged bird sings!”.

questions.prompt: What does the caged bird sense of the world outside in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Sun on the slopes, soft wind in the grass, a river like glass, the first bird and bud, a flower’s scent. The beauty of the free world makes the cage sharper.
evidence: When the wind stirs soft through the springing grass,

questions.prompt: How do the three refrains differ: what the bird “feels,” why it “beats his wing,” why it “sings”?
facilitatorNotes: Feeling, then struggle, then song: the speaker moves from sharing the bird’s longing to its useless fight to the meaning of its music. Each stanza claims a deeper knowledge.
evidence: I know what the caged bird feels!
I know why he beats his wing!

questions.prompt: Why does the bird sing, according to the last stanza? What would a careless listener assume?
facilitatorNotes: Not for “joy or glee” but as a prayer and a plea sent up to Heaven. A careless listener hears cheerfulness; the speaker hears suffering beneath it.
evidence: It is not a carol of joy or glee,
But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings--

questions.prompt: The speaker never names his own cage. Why might Dunbar leave it unstated?
facilitatorNotes: Leaving it open lets the poem speak for many kinds of confinement. Many readers connect it with racial injustice in Dunbar’s America; others with any trapped life. The repeated “I know” insists the knowledge comes from experience.
evidence: And a pain still throbs in the old, old scars

readings.title: Prometheus
readings.challenge: Follow how a poet retells an old myth, then turns it against the poets of his own day.
readings.focus: Dunbar makes Prometheus’s stolen fire the fire of poetry, and complains that modern poets have let it go out.
readings.context: In Greek myth Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans; Zeus punished him terribly. Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, uses the story to talk about poetry. Vestal flames are sacred fires kept burning in a temple; poesy is poetry; celestial ire is the anger of heaven; wroth means angry; ravished means robbed; to “hold in fee” is to own; leaven is yeast, which makes bread rise; Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English poet who wrote a drama about Prometheus; a warbler is a songbird; the lyre is the harp of ancient poets, and the banjo was a popular instrument of Dunbar’s America.

excerpt.locator: “Prometheus,” complete poem; opens “Prometheus stole from Heaven the sacred fire And swept to earth with it o'er land and…”; closes “…their substance tho' we keep their form: We strum our banjo-strings and call them lyres.”.

questions.prompt: According to the first two stanzas, what did Prometheus bring to earth, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Dunbar changes the myth: the fire Prometheus stole lights “the vestal flames of poesy,” and its purpose was to lift human souls. Poetry becomes the gift that makes people more than they are.
evidence: He lit the vestal flames of poesy,
To lift men's souls above their low estate.

questions.prompt: “The fire has been returned to Heaven again!” What does the speaker mean, and why is it said as if it were good news?
facilitatorNotes: Modern poets are so weak that the gods have their fire back: Prometheus suffered for nothing. The speaker pretends the “wrong has been repaired,” which is irony; he means it is a loss.
evidence: 'Twas all in vain that ill Prometheus fared:
The fire has been returned to Heaven again!

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is wrong with the poets of his own time?
facilitatorNotes: They keep the old forms but lack the old power: they “tinkle” where great poets stormed, and call banjo-strumming lyre music. Some readers connect the banjo with Dunbar’s own complaint, in “The Poet,” that the public praised his light dialect verse more than his serious poems.
evidence: We tinkle where old poets used to storm.
We strum our banjo-strings and call them lyres.

questions.prompt: The speaker says “we,” not “they.” Does he include himself? Is this poem an example of what it complains about?
facilitatorNotes: “We” takes the blame with the others, a modest, even bitter, gesture. Yet the poem is itself well made and fiery, which may prove the fire is not quite gone. Students can argue either way from the last stanza.
evidence: We lack their substance tho' we keep their form:
The measure of our songs is our desires:

readings.title: For the Man Who Fails
readings.challenge: Find the line that limits the poem’s praise, and test the argument with examples.
readings.focus: Dunbar writes an ode not for the winner but for the man who fails in a noble cause.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, wrote poems of every mood, from comic to grand. Here he takes the side of those who lose. A snob admires only success and rank; a laurel crown was given to victors in ancient Greece; the cypress, often planted in graveyards, is a sign of mourning; to daunt is to discourage; an ode is a poem of praise.

excerpt.locator: “For the Man Who Fails,” complete poem; opens “The world is a snob, and the man who wins Is the chap for its money's worth: And the lust…”; closes “…fled the strife, And the house of Earth will seem more sweet For the perfume of his life.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is wrong with the way the world treats winners?
facilitatorNotes: The world is “a snob” that values only the winner, and the “lust for success” causes half of the world’s sins. The poem begins by attacking an attitude before praising anyone.
evidence: The world is a snob, and the man who wins
And the lust for success causes half of the sins

questions.prompt: What do the laurel crown and the cypress bough stand for in the second stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The laurel is victory and fame; the cypress is death and mourning. Many heroes die with only the cypress, yet their deeds were as gallant as any victory.
evidence: Twines but for the victor's brow;
With naught but the cypress bough.

questions.prompt: Does the poem praise every failure? Which words limit its praise?
facilitatorNotes: No: only the man who fails “in a noble cause,” who fights for the truth and the right and “has not fled the strife.” Failing because one did not try would not count. Ask students for an example from history or their own lives.
evidence: But the man who fails in a noble cause
If the truth be truth and the right be right,

questions.prompt: How can “the perfume of his life” make the world sweeter if he fails?
facilitatorNotes: His courage and example last after him and influence others, like a scent that lingers in a room. Some readers find this comforting; others may say the world needs causes won, not only fought.
evidence: And the house of Earth will seem more sweet
For the perfume of his life.

readings.title: Harriet Beecher Stowe
readings.challenge: Follow a sonnet’s argument from a book to a war to freedom, and test its large claims.
readings.focus: Dunbar honours the writer whose novel woke the world’s conscience about slavery.
readings.context: Harriet Beecher Stowe (1811–1896) wrote Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852), a novel about enslaved people that sold hundreds of thousands of copies and turned many readers in the North and in Britain against slavery. Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote this sonnet in her honour. A reveille is the bugle call that wakes soldiers; a hovel is a poor hut; complacent means smugly satisfied; transfigured means changed into something finer.

excerpt.locator: “Harriet Beecher Stowe,” complete poem; opens “She told the story, and the whole world wept At wrongs and cruelties it had not known But…”; closes “…Prophet and priestess! At one stroke she gave A race to freedom and herself to fame.”.

questions.prompt: According to the first four lines, what did Stowe do, and how did the world respond?
facilitatorNotes: She told the story of wrongs and cruelties that people “had not known,” and the whole world wept; she woke consciences that had long been asleep. Her only weapon is a voice.
evidence: She told the story, and the whole world wept
She spoke to consciences that long had slept:

questions.prompt: Dunbar compares her message to a bugle call and to a sword leaping from its sheath. What do the two images share?
facilitatorNotes: Both are military: one wakes soldiers, the other is a weapon drawn. The book becomes a call to battle, and justice, which had stayed in its sheath, is suddenly in use. The message also reaches everyone, “From heedless hovel to complacent throne.”
evidence: Her message, Freedom's clear reveille, swept
And from its sheath the sword of justice leapt.

questions.prompt: What is the “fiery wave” around “two peoples,” and how could both come out “transfigured”?
facilitatorNotes: The Civil War, around Black and white Americans. Black Americans came out free; white Americans, the poem suggests, came out freed from the wrong of slavery. Some readers will ask whether the nation was truly changed, given what followed the war; that doubt is worth hearing.
evidence: Around two peoples swelled a fiery wave, But both came forth transfigured from the flame.

questions.prompt: The last line says that at “one stroke” she gave “A race to freedom and herself to fame.” Is that fair to history? What does Dunbar gain by putting it this way?
facilitatorNotes: It overstates: enslaved people who escaped and resisted, Black abolitionists such as Douglass, and soldiers all won freedom, and no novel did it alone. But a tribute compresses, and the balanced line (freedom for them, fame for her) gives a memorable close. Dunbar honours Douglass and the Black soldiers in other poems.
evidence: Prophet and priestess! At one stroke she gave A race to freedom and herself to fame.

readings.title: Little Brown Baby
readings.challenge: Hear a father’s teasing game and find where it turns tender.
readings.focus: Pretending to give the child away becomes a way of showing how fiercely he is loved.
readings.context: In this dialect poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar, a father plays with his small son at the end of the day. Merlasses is molasses; a straggler is a stray; the buggah-man is the bogeyman; a pallet is a bed made up on the floor.
readings.contentNote: A father pretends, in play, to give his child to the bogeyman. Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “Little Brown Baby,” complete poem; opens “Little brown baby wif spa'klin' eyes, Come to yo' pappy an' set on his knee. What you…”; closes “…Wisht you could stay jes' a chile on my breas'-- Little brown baby wif spa'klin' eyes!”.

questions.prompt: Which details show the end of a long, messy, happy day?
facilitatorNotes: Sand pies, a dirty bib, a mouth sticky with molasses, the call to Maria to wipe his hands. The father notices everything about his son.
evidence: What you been doin', suh--makin' san' pies?
Look at dat mouf--dat's merlasses, I bet;

questions.prompt: Why does the father pretend not to know the baby and offer him to the bogeyman?
facilitatorNotes: It is a game: the frightened baby hugs him close, and the father “rescues” him. Mock rejection gives the child the pleasure of being claimed again.
evidence: Pappy do' know you--I b'lieves you 's a tramp;
Dah, now, I t'ought dat you 'd hug me up close.

questions.prompt: What does the father wish in the last lines, and why might he wish it?
facilitatorNotes: That his son could always know ease and clear skies and stay a child on his breast. The wish hints at a hard world waiting; readers may think of the dangers facing a Black child in Dunbar’s America. The tender ending gives weight to the play.
evidence: Wisht you could allus know ease an' cleah skies;
Wisht you could stay jes' a chile on my breas'--

readings.title: Lincoln
readings.challenge: Untangle sentences whose words come in unusual order, and follow a comparison between a president and a musician.
readings.focus: Dunbar pictures the Civil War as a terrible noise and Abraham Lincoln as the master musician who brought it back to harmony.
readings.context: Abraham Lincoln was President of the United States during the Civil War (1861–1865) between the Union states of the North and the Confederate states of the South; the war ended slavery in the United States, and Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865, days after it ended. Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), whose parents had been enslaved in Kentucky, wrote this tribute a generation later. Clam’rous means noisy; unremitting means never stopping; a minor note is a sad musical sound; behest is a command; Homer was the ancient Greek poet of war; a lyre is the harp of ancient poets; discord is clashing sound.
readings.contentNote: The poem refers to the Civil War and to Lincoln’s death.

excerpt.locator: “Lincoln,” complete poem; opens “Hurt was the nation with a mighty wound, And all her ways were filled with clam'rous…”; closes “…learned of thee what Heav'n already knew, And wrote thee down among her treasured few.”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem picture the nation before Lincoln comes? Which side grieves?
facilitatorNotes: The nation is wounded and full of noise; the South wails and the North weeps. Dunbar shows grief on both sides rather than taking one. Ask why a poem about Lincoln might begin this way.
evidence: Hurt was the nation with a mighty wound,
Wailed loud the South with unremitting grief,

questions.prompt: The poem turns the war into music. Find the words of sound and music. What part does Lincoln play?
facilitatorNotes: “Clam’rous sound,” “harshest tone,” “a minor note,” “discord”: the war is noise. Lincoln is the master player who stills the storm and draws “the harmony of peace” from his harp.
evidence: A minor note swelled in the song of life.
Wrenched from his harp the harmony of peace,

questions.prompt: Lincoln “Muted the strings, that made the discord,--Wrong.” What might the “Wrong” be? What does the next line say happened to him?
facilitatorNotes: Dunbar does not name it; most readers take it to be slavery, the wrong behind the war. “Gave his spirit up in thund’rous song” describes his death, as if his assassination were the last great chord. Accept other readings supported by the poem.
evidence: Muted the strings, that made the discord,--Wrong,
And gave his spirit up in thund'rous song.

questions.prompt: Why call Lincoln “The mighty Homer of the lyre of war”? Does the comparison suit a president?
facilitatorNotes: Homer sang the great war of the Greeks; Lincoln, in his speeches and leadership, gave the war its meaning and ended it. Some readers find the comparison grand and fitting; others find it strange to make a politician a poet. Both should point to the poem’s music imagery.
evidence: The mighty Homer of the lyre of war.
Earth learned of thee what Heav'n already knew,

readings.title: Douglass
readings.challenge: Follow a storm-at-sea image through a sonnet addressed to the dead.
readings.focus: The poet calls on a dead leader because the present seems worse than the past he fought through.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote this sonnet several years after Frederick Douglass died in 1895, when Black Americans were losing rights won after the Civil War. Salient means standing out; devious means winding; stark means stiff in death; a bark is a boat.

excerpt.locator: “Douglass,” complete poem; opens “Ah, Douglass, we have fall'n on evil days, Such days as thou, not even thou didst know,…”; closes “…bark, The blast-defying power of thy form, To give us comfort through the lonely dark.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say “we have fall'n on evil days,” worse even than Douglass knew?
facilitatorNotes: Douglass faced slavery, but the speaker sees a new “tempest of dispraise” and quarrelling, with Honor dead at the helm. The claim is startling and asks readers how progress can be lost.
evidence: Ah, Douglass, we have fall'n on evil days,
Such days as thou, not even thou didst know,

questions.prompt: Trace the sea-storm image across the poem.
facilitatorNotes: A battling tide, a tempest, waves of dissension, a dead pilot, a shivering boat in the dark. The nation, or Dunbar’s people, is a small boat in danger without its guide.
evidence: And Honor, the strong pilot, lieth stark,
to guide the shivering bark,

questions.prompt: What does the speaker ask of Douglass, and can a dead man give it? What is the poem really doing?
facilitatorNotes: His voice, his arm, his presence, to comfort them in the dark. He cannot return, so the call expresses grief and need and holds up his example for the living. Readers may hear despair or a summons to new leaders.
evidence: Oh, for thy voice high-sounding o'er the storm,
To give us comfort through the lonely dark.

readings.title: Booker T. Washington
readings.challenge: Find the turn in a sonnet, and see how the portrait shifts from where a man came from to how he moves.
readings.focus: A portrait of a leader, from a cabin door to the prow of a ship.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915) was born enslaved in a cabin in Virginia, worked his way to an education, and in 1881 founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, a school for Black students; he became the best-known Black American of his day. Paul Laurence Dunbar, who knew him, wrote this sonnet. “He who runs may read” echoes the Bible: something written so plainly that a person running past can read it. A peer is an equal; acclaim is praise; a prow is the front of a ship.

excerpt.locator: “Booker T. Washington,” complete poem; opens “The word is writ that he who runs may read. What is the passing breath of earthly fame?…”; closes “…his hip; With one idea foremost in his mind, Like the keen prow of some on-forging ship.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening say true glory is, compared with “earthly fame”?
facilitatorNotes: Fame is only a passing breath. Truly living is to “snatch glory from the hands of blame”: to win honour in spite of those who blame or look down on you.
evidence: What is the passing breath of earthly fame?
But to snatch glory from the hands of blame--

questions.prompt: Lines five to eight tell a life story in four lines. What contrast do they draw?
facilitatorNotes: From a poor Virginia cabin with a “dark and lowly door” to “a peer of princes,” a leader the nation needs. The seed image makes the great man grow from a small beginning.
evidence: A poor Virginia cabin gave the seed,
A peer of princes in the world's acclaim,

questions.prompt: In the last six lines, who might the “hounds” be, and why does he not turn to look at them?
facilitatorNotes: Critics and enemies: people hostile to a Black leader, and also rivals who disagreed with his methods. He keeps to his single purpose; looking back would slow him. The hunting picture makes him a hunted animal who still runs straight.
evidence: Straight on he goes, nor turns to look behind Where hot the hounds come baying at his hip;

questions.prompt: Why might Dunbar end with a ship’s prow? What does the image say about the kind of strength he admires?
facilitatorNotes: A prow is sharp (“keen”) and cuts forward, leading the whole ship: strength as silent, single-minded purpose. Some readers may ask whether a mind with only “one idea” leaves room for doubt or for other people’s ideas; the poem admires it without asking.
evidence: With one idea foremost in his mind, Like the keen prow of some on-forging ship.

readings.title: The Debt
readings.challenge: Follow an extended money metaphor and decide what the poem leaves out on purpose.
readings.focus: One reckless day is paid for with years of regret.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar compresses a life into three short stanzas built on the language of money. Riotous means wild and unrestrained; interest is the extra money owed on a loan.

excerpt.locator: “The Debt,” complete poem; opens “This is the debt I pay Just for one riotous day, Years of regret and grief, Sorrow…”; closes “…bought, Small was the debt I thought, Poor was the loan at best-- God! but the interest!”.

questions.prompt: Which words belong to borrowing and paying, and how do they shape the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Debt, pay, bought, loan, interest. A moment of pleasure becomes a purchase on credit, and regret is the repayment.
evidence: This is the debt I pay
Poor was the loan at best--

questions.prompt: Why is the last line so sudden? What does it reveal?
facilitatorNotes: After calm, even lines, the outburst shows the cost has grown far beyond what the speaker expected: the thing was “slight,” the interest enormous.
evidence: Slight was the thing I bought,
God! but the interest!

questions.prompt: The poem never says what happened on the “riotous day.” Weakness or strength?
facilitatorNotes: Leaving it out lets the poem fit any rash act and keeps attention on the cost. Some readers want the story; others find that the silence makes the regret belong to everyone.
evidence: Just for one riotous day,

readings.title: The Haunted Oak
readings.challenge: Work out who speaks each part, and how letting a tree tell the story changes what we feel.
readings.focus: An oak that witnessed a lynching tells why it can never grow leaves again.
readings.context: Lynching is murder by a mob that takes the law into its own hands. Between the 1880s and the 1930s thousands of Black Americans were lynched, often after a false accusation, and often taken from jail before any trial; the killers were rarely punished. Paul Laurence Dunbar published this ballad in 1900. The oak itself tells most of the story. I trow means I believe; a goad is a spiked stick for driving cattle, and galling means chafing; bedight means dressed up; a throe is a spasm of pain; a ban is a curse.
readings.contentNote: A ballad about a lynching: an innocent man is taken from jail by a masked mob that includes a judge, a doctor and a minister, and is hanged from the oak. The hanging is not described in detail, but the poem is grim; adults should be ready to talk about racial violence in American history.

excerpt.locator: “The Haunted Oak,” complete poem; opens “Pray why are you so bare, so bare, Oh, bough of the old oak-tree; And why, when I go…”; closes “…night stays he; For I feel his curse as a haunted bough, On the trunk of a haunted tree.”.

questions.prompt: Who asks the question in the first stanza, and who answers? Where else do new voices enter?
facilitatorNotes: A passer-by asks why the bough is bare and why it makes him shudder; the oak answers from the second stanza on (“My leaves,” “my veins”). The mob speaks in quotation marks at the jail door. Letting a tree tell it gives the story a witness that cannot be bribed or frightened.
evidence: Pray why are you so bare, so bare, Oh, bough of the old oak-tree;
My leaves were green as the best, I trow,

questions.prompt: How do the riders get the prisoner out of jail? What does their trick show about them?
facilitatorNotes: They claim to be his friends, come to save him from a mob, when they are the mob. The lie uses the very danger they bring, and the jailer opens the door. Cunning, and cowardly: they come by night and in masks.
evidence: We are friends of him whom you hold within,
They have fooled the jailer with lying words,

questions.prompt: Who rides with the mob? Why might Dunbar name a judge, a doctor and a minister?
facilitatorNotes: The town’s most respected men, whose work is justice, healing and mercy, are the killers in disguise. The poem accuses a whole community and its law, not a few outlaws. “The old, old crime” was the charge most often made against lynching victims, an accusation of attacking a white woman; the poem insists this man was guiltless.
evidence: Oh, the judge, he wore a mask of black, And the doctor one of white,
They 'd charged him with the old, old crime,

questions.prompt: At the end, what has happened to the oak, and what happens to the judge? Is this a kind of justice?
facilitatorNotes: The oak is dried and dead, cursed because it bore an innocent man’s death. The judge rides by, goes hunting and lives on, punished only by fear inside him. No court acts, which matches what really happened in most lynchings. Many readers find it unjust that the tree suffers more than the killers, and that may be Dunbar’s point.
evidence: And never more shall leaves come forth On a bough that bears the ban;
And ever the judge rides by, rides by, And goes to hunt the deer,

readings.title: Robert Gould Shaw
readings.challenge: Read the question of a sonnet’s first eight lines and the bitter answer of its last six.
readings.focus: A tribute to a hero turns into a judgment that his sacrifice seems wasted.
readings.context: Robert Gould Shaw, a young white officer from a wealthy Boston family, commanded the 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments of the Civil War, and died with many of his men at Fort Wagner in 1863. Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote this sonnet about forty years later. Pallas is the Greek goddess of wisdom; a fane is a temple; droves are herds or crowds. It is read on Memorial Day, which began after the Civil War as a day for decorating soldiers’ graves.
readings.contentNote: Death in battle. The phrase “unlettered and despised droves” echoes how many people regarded the soldiers at the time.

excerpt.locator: “Robert Gould Shaw,” complete poem; opens “Why was it that the thunder voice of Fate Should call thee, studious, from the classic…”; closes “…thou and those who with thee died for right Have died, the Present teaches, but in vain!”.

questions.prompt: What life does the poem say Shaw left behind?
facilitatorNotes: Study among “classic groves,” where wisdom walks calmly, and home, family and comfort. The poem stresses that he chose danger over ease.
evidence: Should call thee, studious, from the classic groves,
Leave home and kindred and thy spicy loaves,

questions.prompt: What did Shaw go to do, in the poem’s words, and how does it describe the men he led?
facilitatorNotes: To lead them “To manhood's home,” to win recognition of their full humanity. “Unlettered and despised” describes how the world saw them, not Dunbar’s own judgment; discuss the difference.
evidence: To lead th' unlettered and despised droves
To manhood's home and thunder at the gate?

questions.prompt: Why does the last line say they died “in vain”? Does Dunbar want us to accept that?
facilitatorNotes: The present seems to show that the rights they died for have been lost. The ending may be despair, or a protest meant to shame readers into making the sacrifice count; “the Present teaches” suggests the blame lies with the living.
evidence: Have died, the Present teaches, but in vain!

readings.title: Life’s Tragedy
readings.challenge: Rank griefs as the speaker does and test whether you agree.
readings.focus: Coming close to the perfect thing can hurt more than never trying.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar, who published his first book at twenty, writes here about the gap between near success and perfection. A half-tone is the smallest step between notes in Western music; untempered means unrestrained.

excerpt.locator: “Life’s Tragedy,” complete poem; opens “It may be misery not to sing at all And to go silent through the brimming day. It may be…”; closes “…We count our joys not by the things we have, But by what kept us from the perfect thing.”.

questions.prompt: Which sorrows does the first stanza name, and how does it set them aside?
facilitatorNotes: Never singing and never being loved: real griefs, but “deeper griefs than these” are coming. The stanza clears the ground for a surprising claim.
evidence: It may be misery not to sing at all
But deeper griefs than these beset the way.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to lose the key “only by a half-tone”? Why might a small miss hurt more?
facilitatorNotes: Missing perfection by the smallest possible step makes success feel as if it was almost in hand. Readers may compare near misses in music or sport.
evidence: And only by a half-tone lost the key,

questions.prompt: Do you agree with the last two lines about how people count their joys?
facilitatorNotes: The poem says we measure happiness by what kept us from “the perfect thing.” Some readers find this true to regret; others think it is a trap the poem describes rather than recommends.
evidence: We count our joys not by the things we have,
But by what kept us from the perfect thing.

readings.title: Wadin’ in de Crick
readings.challenge: Follow a small adventure stanza by stanza and enjoy the surprise at the end.
readings.focus: A hot day, a creek, a tattletale bird and a mother with a stick.
readings.context: In this dialect poem by Paul Laurence Dunbar, a child skips school on a hot day to wade in the creek (the “crick”). Mussiful means merciful; hookey (hooky) is skipping school; a jay-b’ud is a blue jay, a noisy bird; a tattlah is a tattletale; wilier boughs are willow branches and elum trees are elms; “yo’ Mastah” here means God; scaihed to def means scared to death; bref is breath.
readings.contentNote: A mother comes after her child with a stick, then drops it. Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “Wadin’ in de Crick,” complete poem; opens “Days git wa'm an' wa'mah, School gits mighty dull, Seems lak dese hyeah teachahs Mus'…”; closes “…set down gentle An' she drap huh stick,-- An' fus' t'ing, dey's mammy Wadin' in de crick.”.

questions.prompt: What reasons does the speaker give for skipping school? Which part sounds honest, and which sounds like an excuse?
facilitatorNotes: Warm days, dull school, teachers who ought to be merciful, the air itself calling. The speaker also admits that hooky is wrong and “Ain’t no gent’man’s trick.” Owning up first makes the excuses more charming.
evidence: Hookey's wrong, I know it Ain't no gent'man's trick;
Seems lak dese hyeah teachahs Mus' feel mussiful.

questions.prompt: How do the jay-bird and the trees behave differently? Why does the speaker like the trees better?
facilitatorNotes: The jay is a tattletale who will tell on you; the trees see you too but “don’ chattah,” and their thick trunks are good to hide behind. The speaker gives the creatures personalities, like people in a child’s life.
evidence: Jay-bu'ds sich a tattlah,
But de trees don' chattah,

questions.prompt: What happens in the last stanza, and why is the ending funny?
facilitatorNotes: Mammy comes flying, out of breath, while the child hides; then she sits down gently, drops the stick, and wades in too. The person who came to punish joins the fun, and the refrain that ended every stanza now belongs to her.
evidence: But she set down gentle An' she drap huh stick,--
An' fus' t'ing, dey's mammy Wadin' in de crick.

questions.prompt: Read the second stanza aloud. How do the short lines and the dialect make it sound like the creek, or like a child talking?
facilitatorNotes: Short lines with three beats bounce along; dropped letters make the talk quick and easy; “gu’glin’ / Ovah shiny stones” almost gurgles itself. The voice is breathless and eager, like a child already halfway to the water.
evidence: Dah de watah's gu'glin' Ovah shiny stones,

readings.title: Forever
readings.challenge: Notice how a short poem changes a few words of its first stanza to make its last.
readings.focus: A speaker learns, late and painfully, how long “forever” and how sad “never” can be.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, wrote many short lyrics of love and loss. This one never says what has been lost, so readers must imagine it from the speaker’s words.

excerpt.locator: “Forever,” complete poem; opens “I had not known before Forever was so long a word. The slow stroke of the clock of time I…”; closes “…before That Never was so sad a word, So wrap me in forgetfulness-- I have not heard.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker learn about the word “Forever” in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: How long it is: time now passes slowly, and he hears “The slow stroke of the clock of time.” Something has happened that will last for ever, perhaps a loss or a parting.
evidence: Forever was so long a word.
The slow stroke of the clock of time

questions.prompt: In the third stanza, what relief does the speaker find? Is it real relief?
facilitatorNotes: Only dreams: neither night nor day is quite what it seems, but each can bring “dreams and dreams.” The repetition sounds tired, as if dreams are all that is left. Some readers hear comfort, others sadness.
evidence: But each may bring me this relief--
My dreams and dreams.

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza answer the first? Why change “Forever” to “Never” and end “I have not heard”?
facilitatorNotes: “Forever” becomes “Never,” the other face of the same loss. In the first stanza he “had not heard” the clock; now he asks to be wrapped in forgetfulness, as if he could stop knowing. The poem ends by wishing to un-learn its lesson.
evidence: That Never was so sad a word,
So wrap me in forgetfulness--

readings.title: The Place Where the Rainbow Ends
readings.challenge: Follow how the poem changes the meaning of a familiar legend.
readings.focus: Where the rainbow really ends, and what treasure waits there.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar plays on the old story that a pot of gold lies buried where a rainbow touches the ground; since a rainbow seems to move as you move, no one can ever reach its end. Arabian legends are tales like the Arabian Nights; coffers are treasure chests; pottage is a thick soup or stew; a scoffer is someone who mocks; “truce to the story” means enough of that story.

excerpt.locator: “The Place Where the Rainbow Ends,” complete poem; opens “There's a fabulous story Full of splendor and glory, That Arabian legends transcends; Of…”; closes “…Then truce to the story, Of riches and glory; There's the place where the rainbow ends.”.

questions.prompt: Where have people looked for the treasure, according to the middle stanzas, and what has the search cost them?
facilitatorNotes: In battle, and at the gambling table where dice rattle and men swear. They have spent their blood “recklessly” and still found nothing: the hunt for riches leads to war and vice.
evidence: With the blood we so recklessly spend;
They have sought it in battle,

questions.prompt: What does the speaker mean by finding the place “without motion”?
facilitatorNotes: Not by travelling or chasing, but by staying where he is and being content. Everyone else runs after the rainbow; he lets its end come to him.
evidence: And I have a notion, To find without motion,

questions.prompt: What is in the pot and where is the place, in the last two stanzas? Why might Dunbar turn “pot” into “pottage”?
facilitatorNotes: A pot of stew instead of gold, a cottage instead of a palace, and joy, love and friends as the wealth. The pun brings the legend down to everyday life: the real treasure is ordinary.
evidence: The pot may hold pottage,
And I shall find wealth in my friends;

questions.prompt: The speaker admits that gold “has a power it lends.” Does that admission make his choice more convincing or less?
facilitatorNotes: More, because he is not naive: he knows what money can do and chooses otherwise. Less, some may say, because it is easy to scorn wealth you do not have, and he expects to be mocked (“spite of the scoffer”). Both views can be argued from the poem.
evidence: Though gold has a power it lends;
But spite of the scoffer,

readings.title: Limitations
readings.challenge: Find the single piece of advice behind several different comparisons.
readings.focus: Do not pretend to be more than you are: people will find you out.
readings.context: In this dialect poem Paul Laurence Dunbar gives advice through homely comparisons. Fe’ means for; a teenchy bit is a tiny bit; victuals (said “vittles”) are food; ’spicious means suspicious; a pint is a small measure and a bar’l (barrel) a large one; idees are ideas. A mockingbird is famous for its many beautiful songs; a crow only caws.
readings.contentNote: Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “Limitations,” complete poem; opens “Ef you's only got de powah fe' to blow a little whistle, Keep ermong de people wid de…”; closes “…t'ing in de country dat I evah hyahed-- A crow dot sat a-squawkin', "I's a mockin'-bird."”.

questions.prompt: Each stanza compares a person to something small pretending to be big. Name the comparisons, including the last one.
facilitatorNotes: A little whistle squeaking against a great horn; a tiny bit of food called a feast; a half-pint mind claiming to be a barrel; and a crow announcing that it is a mockingbird.
evidence: A-squeakin' of yo' whistle 'g'inst a gread big ho'n.
Don' go roun' a-sayin' hit's a bar'l;

questions.prompt: What happens, in each stanza, to people who pretend?
facilitatorNotes: Their finest feelings land in a bed of thistles; suspicious neighbours come peering for scraps; people test them, catch the lie and twist their words. Pretending leads to being found out and laughed at.
evidence: Fe' de folks is mighty 'spicious, an' dey's ap' to come apeerin',
'Ca'se de people gwine to test you, an' dey'll fin' out you's a-lyin',

questions.prompt: Why is the crow the “wuss t’ing” the speaker ever heard?
facilitatorNotes: Because its own squawk disproves the boast the moment it speaks. Saving the funniest picture for last makes the lesson stick: a pretender gives himself away.
evidence: A crow dot sat a-squawkin', "I's a mockin'-bird."

questions.prompt: Is the poem telling people to stay small, or to be honest? Could its advice be misused?
facilitatorNotes: Its target is boasting and pretending, not ambition. But “Keep ermong de people wid de whistles” could be heard as “stay in your place,” and people have used such advice to hold others back; Dunbar himself rose far beyond what others expected of him. Good answers separate being honest about your powers from accepting limits others set.
evidence: Keep ermong de people wid de whistles.

readings.title: The Masters
readings.challenge: Follow a poem built of two questions and two answers, and notice what changes between them.
readings.focus: Love rules life while it is a hot struggle; Death rules it at sunset, whoever has won.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906), an African American poet from Dayton, Ohio, often wrote short songs in ballad rhythm. A fray is a fight; a monarch’s sway is a king’s rule; to wend is to go; rife means everywhere; Death is often pictured as a reaper with a scythe, a long curved blade for cutting grain; a pruning-knife cuts branches from trees.

excerpt.locator: “The Masters,” complete poem; opens “Oh, who is the Lord of the land of life, When hotly goes the fray? When, fierce we smile…”; closes “…hot race is run. Meet then his scythe and, pruning-knife When the fray is lost or won.”.

questions.prompt: The poem asks two questions. What are they, and what time of life goes with each?
facilitatorNotes: Who rules life “When hotly goes the fray,” in the struggle of youth and middle life, and who rules “At setting of the sun,” at the end. The repeated question form makes the two answers mirror each other.
evidence: When hotly goes the fray?
At setting of the sun?

questions.prompt: Why might Love be “Lord of the land of life” during the struggle?
facilitatorNotes: Love drives what people work and fight for, the “wish of maid and wife”: it is what we obey while we are busy living. Readers may suggest other rulers, such as ambition, and test them against the poem.
evidence: Oh, Love is the Lord of the land of life
He wends with wish of maid and wife,

questions.prompt: How is Death’s rule described? Does the last line make Death fair, cruel or neither?
facilitatorNotes: Death comes with his scythe “When the fray is lost or won”: winning or losing makes no difference. Some readers find that fair, since all are equal at the end; others find it grim. The poem does not judge; it simply states.
evidence: Then Death is the Lord of the land of life,
When the fray is lost or won.

readings.title: Equipment
readings.challenge: Listen to a worker speaking to God, and decide whether he is proud, humble, or both.
readings.focus: A maker offers his work to the Master who gave him his tools, and asks to be judged fairly.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar died of tuberculosis at thirty-three, after writing poems, stories and novels; many readers praised only his dialect poems, which frustrated him. Here a worker speaks to God. Equipment means the gifts and tools a person is given; wrought is an old past tense of work, meaning made or fashioned; raucous means harsh and loud; railing is scolding or mockery.

excerpt.locator: “Equipment,” complete poem; opens “With what thou gavest me, O Master, I have wrought. Such chances, such abilities, To see…”; closes “…If they are few, is the workmanship true? Try them and weigh me, whate'er be my due!”.

questions.prompt: Who is the “Master,” and what did he give the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: God, addressed as “O Master” and later “ah God!” He gave chances and abilities, and the first impulse and plan of the work; the speaker could not see where it would end.
evidence: With what thou gavest me, O Master, I have wrought.
Thine was the impulse, thine the forming thought.

questions.prompt: The speaker says his work was not “hard up striving after glory.” How does he say he worked instead?
facilitatorNotes: Not grabbing at success, winning and losing, or shouting back at the world’s mockery, but “simply and humbly,” like a mason or carpenter working stone and wood, to make things that might seem good to God.
evidence: Raging me back at the world's raucous railing.
Simply and humbly from stone and from wood,

questions.prompt: “If they are little, ah God! but the cost.” What might the cost be?
facilitatorNotes: Effort, suffering, time, and things given up, “the all that is lost,” which only God knows. Some readers connect this with Dunbar’s short, hard-working life and his wish to be valued for all his work; the poem itself names no details.
evidence: If they are little, ah God! but the cost,
Who but thou knowest the all that is lost!

questions.prompt: Why does the poem end with “Try them and weigh me”? Is the speaker proud, humble, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He asks to be judged by how true the workmanship is, not by how big or how many the works are, and he accepts whatever he deserves. Humble about the size of his work, proud of its honesty: good answers find both in the last lines.
evidence: If they are few, is the workmanship true?
Try them and weigh me, whate'er be my due!

readings.title: The King Is Dead
readings.challenge: Follow a speaker who mourns the old year as if it were a king and a friend, while everyone around him cheers the new one.
readings.focus: Saying goodbye to a year means weighing what it gave against what it took.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) wrote poems for many turning points of the calendar. When a king died, heralds cried “The king is dead! long live the king!”, so that mourning the old ruler and greeting the new one happened in the same breath. A bier is the stand on which a coffin rests; manifold means many; fain means glad or willing. It is read on New Year’s Day, when the old year has just ended.

excerpt.locator: “The King Is Dead,” complete poem; opens “Aye, lay him in his grave, the old dead year! His life is lived--fulfilled his destiny.…”; closes “…end; We cry e'en as thy footsteps downward tend: "The king is dead! long live the king!"”.

questions.prompt: Who is the “king” in the title, and how do you know?
facilitatorNotes: The old year, which has just ended. The first line names him “the old dead year,” and the poem treats him as a person who has lived out his “destiny” and is being buried.
evidence: Aye, lay him in his grave, the old dead year!

questions.prompt: The second stanza is a string of questions. What answer does the speaker expect, and what does he want his listener to feel?
facilitatorNotes: He expects “yes”: the year was kind and gave enough love, laughter and clear skies. The questions are meant to shame an ungrateful listener into a little gratitude and sorrow, the “tribute of a sigh” the first stanza asks for.
evidence: Was he not kind to you, this dead old year?
How, then, of him who dies, could you ask more?

questions.prompt: The speaker admits the year brought him pain and “sorrows manifold.” Why does he still forgive it?
facilitatorNotes: Because the same year that hurt him also healed older hurts: “He brought me new wounds, but he healed the old.” Good answers notice the balance inside that one line. Some readers see the speaker accepting that every year brings both; others see time itself as the healer.
evidence: It is not well to hate him for the pain
He brought me new wounds, but he healed the old.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with the old cry “The king is dead! long live the king!” Is the ending sad, hopeful, or both?
facilitatorNotes: Both. The speaker gives only “one little sigh” while his companions sing, and admits the old year is “so soon forgotten”; yet the same cry welcomes the new year at once. Accept either emphasis if it rests on the contrast between the single sigh and the singing.
evidence: One little sigh while my companions sing.
Thou art so soon forgotten in the end;

readings.title: Columbian Ode
readings.challenge: Read a celebration poem closely enough to see whose story it tells and whose it leaves out.
readings.focus: An ode in praise of Columbus pictures the Americas before 1492 as an empty land waiting to be found.
readings.context: Columbus Day marks Christopher Columbus’s landing in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492. In 1892–93 the United States celebrated the four hundredth anniversary, above all at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where the young Paul Laurence Dunbar (1872–1906) worked for Frederick Douglass at the Haiti pavilion. Dunbar’s ode, which begins “Four hundred years ago,” belongs to that celebration. Millions of people already lived in the Americas in 1492. An ode is a formal poem of praise. Conned means studied; thriftless means wasteful; the Genoese is Columbus, born in Genoa; a bark is a ship; Bruin is a name for a bear; mien means appearance.
readings.contentNote: Calls the Native peoples of North America “men of savage mien” and treats their homelands as wilderness; the last question examines that view.

excerpt.locator: “Columbian Ode,” complete poem; opens “Four hundred years ago a tangled waste Lay sleeping on the west Atlantic's side; Their…”; closes “…moved the forest-foliage banner green, Now flutters in the breeze the stars and stripes!”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza picture the Americas and Europe four hundred years before the poem? What does each picture suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The Americas are “a tangled waste” lying asleep. Europe is busy, loving, laboring and daring, but content with old charts and ignorant of other lands. The poem makes Europe active yet narrow, and the Americas empty and waiting.
evidence: Four hundred years ago a tangled waste
Lay sleeping on the west Atlantic's side;

questions.prompt: In the second section, Nature is a mother hiding a child. Who is the child, and why might Dunbar picture the land this way?
facilitatorNotes: The child is the American continent, which grows into “a mighty land.” The image makes the land precious and cared for before Columbus came, and makes its growth seem natural and destined. Some students will notice that a mother and an infant leave no room for the people already living there.
evidence: Another offspring, fine and fair to view,--
And changed the infant to a mighty land.

questions.prompt: What does the third section praise in Columbus, and how do light and dark help?
