facilitatorNotes: Courage against “fears and foes” and against the unknown. He is the “dauntless darer of the rayless dark,” and the whole world sails with him “to eternal light,” so his voyage becomes a victory for all humanity.
evidence: Who dared to try, in spite of fears and foes,
O dauntless darer of the rayless dark,

questions.prompt: The last lines list what replaced the wilderness. What, and whom, does the poem say was replaced? Is that a fair account of the people who lived there?
facilitatorNotes: Deer-haunts became tilled fields, the bear’s den a schoolhouse, the wigwam a chapel, and “men of savage mien” the “noblest types.” The wigwam shows that people lived there, yet the poem counts them as part of the wilderness to be cleared. A defensible answer finds the account one-sided: it celebrates progress and leaves out the Native nations’ own homes, farms and losses. Some readers add that a young Black poet in 1893 was writing in the public language of the celebration; accept answers that weigh both.
evidence: And where the wigwam stood the chapel stands;
The place that nurtured men of savage mien

readings.title: The Boogah Man
readings.challenge: Read a spooky night-time song aloud and work out who is singing it, to whom, and why.
readings.focus: A grown-up uses a pretend monster to settle a child at bedtime, and the song ends by promising safety.
readings.context: Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote many poems in the dialect of Black Southern speech as writers of his time set it down; read them aloud and listen for the rhythm. A boogah man is a bogeyman, an imaginary night creature used to frighten children into behaving. Keerful is careful; des a drappin’ pin is just a dropping pin; peepers are eyes; kivers are covers; a “Lay me” is the bedtime prayer that begins “Now I lay me down to sleep.” It is read at Halloween, the night for frights that are not too serious.
readings.contentNote: Uses historical literary dialect; read it for voice and rhythm, not as caricature.

excerpt.locator: “The Boogah Man,” complete poem; opens “W'en de evenin' shadders Come a-glidin' down, Fallin' black an' heavy Ovah hill an' town,…”; closes “…Den de rain kin pattah Win' blow lak a fan, But you need n' bothah 'Bout de Boogah Man!”.

questions.prompt: What sounds and sights does the speaker say come with the Boogah Man? Why might they all be things you could really hear on a dark night?
facilitatorNotes: Falling shadows, a strange sound across the land, the wind shivering down a lane, the patter of rain, an owl hooting. Every sign is an ordinary night noise, so the “monster” is really the dark itself, filled in by a listening child’s imagination.
evidence: W'en de win 's a-shiverin'
W'en de owl's a-hootin',

questions.prompt: The italic chorus sounds different from the other stanzas. What is it imitating, and what does it tell the child to do?
facilitatorNotes: It imitates the Boogah Man’s call, “Woo-oo,” and tells the child to hide its eyes and wish for daylight. Read aloud, it turns the poem into a game of fright, like a ghost story told with sound effects. Some readers hear teasing; others hear something really scary for a small child.
evidence: Hide yo' little peepers 'hind yo' han;
Callin' of de Boogah Man.

questions.prompt: “Don’ you wish, my honey, / Dat you had been good?” Who is “honey,” and how does that word change the threat?
facilitatorNotes: A small child, being put to bed by someone who loves it. The tender word shows that the speaker is not cruel: the fright is part of a bedtime game, and the speaker may be enjoying it as much as the child.
evidence: Don' you wish, my honey,
Dat you had been good?

questions.prompt: In the last stanza, what must the child do so that it “need n’ bothah” about the Boogah Man? What does this show about why grown-ups tell such stories?
facilitatorNotes: Love mammy, mind pap, stay in Sukey’s lap, and say the bedtime prayer every night. The scary figure turns out to be a way of getting a child to behave and settle down; once the child is good and tucked in, wind and rain can do no harm. Students may call the poem gentle, because the threat ends in comfort, or a little unfair, because fear is used to make children obey.
evidence: Ef you loves yo' mammy,
'Bout de Boogah Man!

readings.title: A Thanksgiving Poem
readings.challenge: Follow a harvest prayer from thanks for full bins to the admission that the gifts were not earned.
readings.focus: A community gives thanks for a good harvest and for safety, and asks what it owes in return.
readings.context: Thanksgiving is the American harvest holiday of late November, kept nationally every year since Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation of 1863. Paul Laurence Dunbar writes this poem as a hymn of thanks spoken by a whole community, “we,” to God. Blight is a plant disease; goodly store is a good supply; pestilence is a deadly epidemic; erring means doing wrong; nigh means near; to pall is to grow weak; consecrate means to dedicate to God.

excerpt.locator: “A Thanksgiving Poem,” complete poem; opens “The sun hath shed its kindly light, Our harvesting is gladly o'er Our fields have felt no…”; closes “…pall; Though we should strive years without end, We could not thank thee for them all.”.

questions.prompt: List what the first two stanzas give thanks for. Which are gifts received, and which are dangers escaped?
facilitatorNotes: Gifts: sunlight, a finished harvest, full bins. Dangers escaped: blight, pestilence, fire, flood and the sword, meaning war. A thankful community remembers both what it has and what did not happen to it.
evidence: Our bins are filled with goodly store.
From pestilence, fire, flood, and sword

questions.prompt: In the third and fourth stanzas the speakers say their own merits did not earn these gifts. Why would people giving thanks say this about themselves?
facilitatorNotes: They call themselves “erring children” who hid from God; the blessings came from mercy, not as wages. Humility makes the thanks sincere, because a gift you did not earn calls for more gratitude than pay you are owed. Some students may find the self-blame too harsh; accept that if they ground it in the lines.
evidence: We feel that had our merits been
No deed of ours hath brought us grace;

questions.prompt: Where is God pictured in the fifth and sixth stanzas, and which image connects him with the farmers of the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Above, in the sky, with an open hand and a “watchful eye.” His “storehouse in the sky” echoes the farmers’ full bins, making God the great provider whose harvest fills theirs.
evidence: And from thy storehouse in the sky
Hast scattered plenty everywhere.

questions.prompt: The last stanza says the speakers “could not thank thee for them all.” How does the poem answer that problem?
facilitatorNotes: Words cannot repay the gifts, so the speakers promise their lives instead: “To thee we consecrate our days,” and each mind is to be God’s temple. Thanks become a way of living, not only a song. Accept other readings grounded in the last two stanzas.
evidence: To thee we consecrate our days;
We could not thank thee for them all.
